summary.summary: This is Cyngor Gwynedd's own 2025/26 Statement of Accounts, still marked 'Subject to Audit', going to the council's Governance and Audit Committee. The balance sheet is solid: long-term borrowing fell from £90.1m to £69.4m over the year, total reserves grew from £592.7m to £644.6m, and the unearmarked General Fund balance nearly doubled from £7.9m to £14.5m after a deliberate top-up. The Capital Financing Requirement rose to £188.5m (from £179.9m) even as external borrowing fell, meaning the council is increasingly relying on internal borrowing rather than new external debt. The narrative notes real budget pressure — a £6.6m in-year overspend concentrated in adult/children's care and waste — but there is no exceptional financial support, capitalisation direction, or section 114-type language anywhere in the document.

news_drafts.headline: North Wales CJC forecasts £39,874 net overspend for 2026/27, with £516,625 on unbudgeted consultants
news_drafts.lead:
The North Wales Corporate Joint Committee (CJC) expects to end 2026/27 with a net overspend of £39,874, according to its July review report before the Governance and Audit Sub-committee on 15 October. The extra cost will be met from reserves, the money the body has set aside, on top of a £624,590 transfer already approved.

The small net figure sits on a larger movement in gross spending. Budgeted expenditure of £1,959,770 is forecast to reach £2,589,644, an overspend of £629,874, or 32%. The main driver is £516,625 on external consultants, against a budget of nothing: £254,400 for programme management, £236,225 for legal work and £26,000 for business advisers. Spending on supplies and services is also forecast to be £435,864 above budget.

Reserves stood at £1,636,007 on 31 March 2026 and are estimated at £971,543 by 31 March 2027. The CJC's statutory finance officer says reserves are expected to be needed for future budgets, as the CJC's resourcing requirements increase and future grants have not been confirmed.

news_drafts.headline: Gwynedd has £16m of new capital money against £19.76m of requests, and built 118 homes against 247
news_drafts.lead:
Gwynedd Council's Cabinet has been told it has about £16m in additional money for capital spending (spending on things that last, such as buildings and flood defences) but requests from education and flood prevention projects come to £19.76m, a gap of £3.76m. The council's Capital Strategy says: "Given that there is currently £16M of additional resource available, it is not possible to fund everything and therefore, there will be a need to prioritise."

The £16m has built up since the council approved its 2024-2034 Asset Plan. It comes from capital grants, receipts, and £3.5m released by de-committing the Health and Care Hub project. The papers do not say which schemes will be funded or dropped.

A separate report to the meeting, the Annual Monitoring Report, covers housing. It records 118 homes completed in the Gwynedd Planning Authority area in 2025/26. That is 129 fewer than the annual average requirement of 247 (52.2% below) and 107 fewer than the forecast trajectory of 225. Since the local plan was adopted in 2017, 2,805 homes have been completed against a trajectory of 3,712, which is 24.4% below.

news_drafts.headline: Gwynedd took out no new loans in first quarter of 2026/27, leaving borrowing at £73.9m
news_drafts.lead:
Gwynedd Council took out no new loans in the first quarter of 2026/27, and its total borrowing stood at £73.9m, unchanged from 31 March. The figures are in the treasury management update (the report on how the council borrows and invests its spare cash) that went to its Governance and Audit Committee on 29 September.

The council says this is deliberate. It is using what is known as internal borrowing, meaning it pays for long-lasting spending from its own cash rather than taking a loan. This saves interest but uses up the cash cushion. The paper says the approach keeps borrowing below the council's underlying need.

The paper says the strategy "enabled the Council to reduce net borrowing costs (despite foregoing investment income) and reduce overall treasury risk". In other words, cash that is spent in place of a loan no longer earns interest as an investment, but the council judges the interest it saves on loans to be worth more. Its net investments stood at £11.4m.

findings.committee: North Wales CJC Governance & Audit Sub-committee
findings.headline: Annual Governance Statement submitted late to audit, creating resource and schedule pressures
findings.detail: The Annual Governance Statement was not provided with the draft financial statements and submitted late in the audit process, creating additional resourcing and timetable pressures. The auditor expects the AGS to be prepared and submitted alongside draft accounts in future years to support timely and efficient audit completion.
findings.matters: Timely submission of audit documentation is essential for maintaining schedule integrity and controlling audit costs. Late submissions can cascade delays in publication of audited accounts.
findings.quote: The Annual Governance Statement (AGS) was not provided alongside the draft financial statements and was submitted at a late stage of the audit process. This created additional resourcing and timetable pressures in completing the necessary audit work on the AGS before the North Wales CJC's consideration of the financial statements.

findings.committee: North Wales CJC Governance & Audit Sub-committee
findings.headline: First full year audit of North Wales CJC required more work than original estimate due to transition complexity
findings.detail: The 2025-26 audit was the first full year following transfer of NWEAB arrangements to the CJC on 1 April 2025. The audit required additional work beyond the original fee estimate of £34,832 to understand new governance arrangements, reporting requirements, accounting treatments, and to audit opening balances transferred to the entity. The final fee is to be agreed with the Statutory Finance Officer.
findings.matters: Finance directors managing transitions of public bodies need visibility of audit cost implications when establishing new accounting systems and governance arrangements, which can significantly exceed initial estimates.
findings.quote: As this was the first year that the North Wales CJC prepared a full set of financial statements following the transfer of the North Wales Economic Ambition Board arrangements on 1 April 2025, the audit involved more work than originally anticipated. Additional work was required to understand and evaluate the new governance arrangements, reporting requirements, accounting treatments, and the opening balances transferred to the CJC.

findings.committee: North Wales CJC Governance & Audit Sub-committee
findings.headline: Welsh Government did not confirm accounting treatment for Parc Bryn Cegin collaborative arrangement
findings.detail: The auditor identified uncertainty regarding the accounting treatment of the CJC's collaborative agreement with Welsh Government for Parc Bryn Cegin, where Welsh Government provides land and the CJC provides funding. Welsh Government did not respond to clarification requests before the audit concluded, leaving the treatment unresolved. The auditor was unable to fully conclude on its appropriateness, though notes potential impact is not expected to be material to 2025-26 accounts. The matter is flagged for monitoring as the arrangement develops.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders need visibility of significant material-by-nature transactions with key funders where accounting treatment is unresolved, as this affects balance sheet presentation and creates uncertainty for future reporting.
findings.quote: During the audit, we identified uncertainty regarding the accounting treatment of the collaborative agreement with Welsh Government for Parc Bryn Cegin. We sought clarification from Welsh Government on the appropriate accounting treatment; however, a response had not been received before completion of our audit work. Consequently, we were unable to conclude fully on whether the treatment adopted by the CJC is appropriate.

findings.committee: North Wales CJC Governance & Audit Sub-committee
findings.headline: Net budget overspend of £39,874 after accounting for additional grants and reserve contribution
findings.detail: Despite the £629,874 gross expenditure overspend, additional grant income of £590,000 combined with the budgeted reserve contribution of £624,590 holds the net expenditure overspend to £39,874. The organisation is forecast to draw £624,590 from reserves (consistent with budget), indicating structural dependence on reserve funding to balance the operating account.
findings.matters: The net position masks reliance on both reserves and discretionary grant income to balance finances. A lender needs to assess reserve sustainability and whether the organisation can continue funding the gap between operating expenditure and core income.
findings.figures: Total Net Expenditure Budget £1,015,180, Forecast £1,055,054, Overspend £39,874. Reserve contribution £624,590 in both budget and forecast.

findings.committee: North Wales CJC Governance & Audit Sub-committee
findings.headline: Additional Welsh Government grant funding of £370,000 transport grant and new £200,000 Local Growth Fund grant partially offset expenditure overspend
findings.detail: The Regional Transport Plan grant came in at £470,000 forecast versus £100,000 budgeted, a favourable variance of £370,000. Additionally, a Local Growth Fund grant of £200,000 was received against zero budget, and interest on balances improved by £20,000. Total additional income of £590,000 significantly reduces the net budget pressure.
findings.matters: Grant income variances indicate either conservative original budgeting or changed government funding decisions. While the additional funds improve the position, reliance on grant funding that exceeds budget creates cash flow uncertainty and indicates external factors beyond the organisation's control are critical to financial stability.
